§ 19. ''Reversion of an Algebraic Integral.''—In a limited number of cases the equation <math>u = \int_{z_0}^{z} \text{H}(z)dz</math>, in which <math>\text{H}(z)</math> is an algebraic function of <math>z</math>, defines <math>z</math> as a single valued function of <math>u</math>. Several cases of this have been mentioned in the previous section; from what was previously proved under § 14, ''Doubly Periodic Functions'', it appears that it is necessary for this that the integral should have at most two linearly independent additive constants of indeterminateness; for instance, for an integral
{{block center|<math>u = \int_{z_0}^{z} [(z-a)(z-b)(z-c)(z-d)(z-e)(z-f)]^{-\frac{1}{2}}dz,</math>}}
there are three such constants, of the form <math>\text{A}-\text{B}</math>, <math>\text{A}-\text{C}</math>, <math>\text{A}-\text{D}</math>, which are not connected by any linear equation with integral coefficients, and <math>z</math> is not a single valued function of <math>u</math>.

§ 20. ''Elliptic Integrals.''—An integral of the form <math>\int \text{R}(z, s)dz</math>, where <math>s</math> denotes the square root of a quartic polynomial in <math>z</math>, which may reduce to a cubic polynomial, and <math>\text{R}</math> denotes a

When <math>z</math> is in the neighbourhood of any finite value <math>z_0</math> for which the radical <math>s</math> is not zero, if we put <math>z-z_0=t</math>, we can find <math>s-s_0=</math> a power series in <math>t</math>, say <math>s=s_0+\text{Q}(t)</math>; when <math>z</math> is in the neighbourhood of a value, <math>a</math>, for which <math>s</math> vanishes, if we put <math>z=a+t^2</math>, we shall obtain <math>s=t\text{Q}(t)</math>, where <math>\text{Q}(t)</math> is a power series in <math>t</math>; when <math>z</math> is very large and <math>s^2</math> is a quartic polynomial in <math>z</math>, if we put <math>z^{-1}=t</math>, we shall find <math>s^{-1}=t^2\text{Q}(t)</math>; when <math>z</math> is very large and <math>s^2</math> is a cubic polynomial in <math>z</math>, if we put <math>z^{-1}=t^2</math>, we shall find <math>s^{-1}=t^3\text{Q}(t)</math>. In each of these cases, of the integrals <math>\text{J}_1</math>, <math>\text{J}_2</math>, <math>\text{J}_3</math>, the subject of integration has been chosen so that when the integral is written near its point of infinity in the form <math>\int[\text{A}t^{-2}+\text{B}t^{-1}+\text{Q}(t)]dt</math>, the coefficient <math>\text{B}</math> is zero, so that the infinity is of algebraic kind, and so that, when there are two signs distinguishable for the critical value of <math>z</math>, the integral becomes infinite for only one of these. If then we have any elliptic integral having algebraic infinities we can, by subtraction from it of an appropriate sum of constant multiples of <math>\text{J}_1</math>, <math>\text{J}_2</math>, <math>\text{J}_3</math> and their differential coefficients just written down, obtain, as the result, an integral without algebraic infinities. But, in fact, if <math>\text{J}</math>, <math>\text{J}^1</math> denote any two of the three integrals <math>\text{J}_1</math>, <math>\text{J}_2</math>, <math>\text{J}_3</math>, there exists an equation <math>\text{AJ}+\text{BJ}'+\text{C}fs^{-1}dz=</math>rational function of <math>s</math>, <math>z</math>, where <math>\text{A},\text{B},\text{C}</math> are properly chosen constants. For the rational function

{{block center|<math>\frac{s+s_0}{z-z_0}+z\sqrt{a_0}</math>}}

is at once found to become infinite for <math>(z_0, s_0)</math>, not for <math>(z_0, -s_0)</math>, its infinite part for the first point being <math>2s/(z-z_0)</math>, and to become infinite for <math>z</math> infinitely large, and one sign of <math>s</math> only when these are separable, its infinite part there being <math>2z\sqrt{a_0}</math> or <math>2\sqrt{a_1}\sqrt{z}</math> when <math>a_0=0</math>. Such an integral <math>\text{H} = \int \text{R}(z, s) dz</math> does not exist, however, as we at once find by writing <math>\text{R}(z, s) = \text{P}(z) + s\text{Q}(z)</math>, where <math>\text{P}(z)</math>, <math>\text{Q}(z)</math> are rational functions of <math>z</math>, and examining the forms possible for these in order that the integral may have only the specified infinity. An analogous theorem holds for rational functions of <math>z</math> and <math>s</math>; there exists no rational function which is finite for finite values of <math>z</math> and is infinite only for <math>z=\infty</math> for one sign of <math>s</math> and to the first order only; but there exists a rational function infinite in all to the first order for each of two or more pairs <math>(z, s)</math>, however they may be situated, or infinite to the second order for an arbitrary pair <math>(z,s)</math>; and any rational function may be formed by a sum of constant multiples of functions such as

{{block center|<math>\frac{s+s_0}{z-z_0}+z\sqrt{a_0}</math> or <math>\frac{s}{z-\theta}+z\sqrt{a_0}</math>}}

and their differential coefficients.

The consideration of elliptic integrals is therefore reducible to that of the three

{{block center|<math>u=\int\frac{dz}{s},\ \ \text{J}=\int\left(\frac{a_0z^2+2a_1z}{s}+z\sqrt{a_0}\right)dz,\ \ \text{P}=\int\left(\frac{s+s_0}{z-z_0}+z\sqrt{a_0}\right)\frac{dz}{2s}</math>}}

respectively of the first, second and third kind. Now the equation <math>s^2=a_0z^4+\dots=a_0(z-\theta)(z-\phi)(z-\psi)(z-\chi)</math>, by putting

{{block center|<math>y=2s(z-\theta)^{-2}[a_0(\theta-\phi)(\theta-\psi)(\theta-\chi)]^{-\frac{1}{2}}</math>}}

{{block center|<math>x=\frac{1}{z-\theta}+\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{1}{\theta-\phi}+\frac{1}{\theta-\psi}+\frac{1}{\theta-\chi}\right)</math>}}

is at once reduced to the form <math>y^2=4x^3-g_2x-g_3=4(x-e_1)(x-e_2(x-e_3)</math>, say; and these equations enable us to express <math>s</math> and <math>z</math> rationally in terms of <math>x</math> and <math>y</math>. It is therefore sufficient to consider three elliptic integrals

{{block center|<math>u=\int\frac{dx}{y},\ \ \text{J}=\int\frac{xdx}{y},\ \ \text{P}=\int\frac{y+y_0}{x-x_0}\frac{dx}{2y}.</math>}}

Of these consider the first, putting

{{block center|<math>u=\int_{(x)}^{(\infty)}\frac{dx}{y},</math>}}

where the limits involve not only a value for <math>x</math>, but a definite sign for the radical <math>y</math>. When <math>x</math> is very large, if we put <math>x^{-1}=t^2, y^{-1}=2t^3(1-\tfrac{1}{4}g_2t^4-\tfrac{1}{4}g_3t^6)^{-\frac{1}{2}}</math>, we have

{{block center|<math>u=\int_0^t(1+\tfrac{1}{8}g_2t^4+\dots)dt=t+\tfrac{1}{40}g_2t^5+\dots,</math>}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
